title: A Choir for the Bell
premise: Wren Joubert has spent years mapping the unmapped tunnels beneath the village of Saint-Aubin, keeping meticulous counts of doors and lights to hold their own fractured memory together. When the church bell rings one night—a bell melted down in 1911—the sound begins erasing things: names, faces, Wren's own carefully kept records. The tunnels are a memory the village buried, and in 1974 Wren's grandfather helped steal the bell's clapper and hide it in the flooded well to silence what the village had done. To stop the erasure, Wren must descend before the well refills with spring meltwater, return the clapper, and choose between the loyalty that protected their family's secret and the truth that will let the village—and Wren—remember who they are. In the end, Wren rings the restored bell themselves, letting the past flood back in, and the village must live with everything it buried.
about_author: Isandro Lockridge is a former surveyor's assistant who spent a decade documenting abandoned infrastructure across rural France before turning to horror. They write at night, in buildings with the doors counted.

chapters.title: The Doors I Count
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren maps the tunnels beneath Saint-Aubin, establishing their ritual: lights on, doors counted, everything written down to keep their patchy memory anchored. The chapter closes with a strange detail—thirteen doors where twelve were yesterday. Emotional beat: quiet competence shadowed by unease.

chapters.title: A Bell with No Bell
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. At midnight, the church bell rings. Wren checks the tower: the belfry is empty, melted down in 1911 per every record. Old villagers on the street don't seem to hear it—or pretend not to. Emotional beat: vertigo, the first crack in Wren's ordered world.

chapters.title: What the Parish Register Forgot
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. In the archive, pages of the parish register are blank where 1911 should be, and the priest, Father Anselme, flinches at the word 'bell.' Wren finds a marginal note: 'returned to the water.' Emotional beat: the thrill of a real mystery curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Hands
chapters.summary: Wren visits their grandmother Odile, whose dementia makes her memory unreliable—yet she hums the bell's note perfectly and says, 'Don't let it finish counting you.' Wren realizes her lost memories and the bell's ringing are entangled. Emotional beat: tenderness and fear braided together.

chapters.title: The Thirteenth Door
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, tunnels. Wren finds a door in the tunnels that isn't on any survey and wasn't there before—a door that hums with the bell's resonance. Inside, the air is 1974. Emotional beat: fascination giving way to the sense of being invited, or lured.

chapters.title: The Man Who Counts Backwards
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren encounters Émile, a hollow-eyed man in the tunnels who has been 'counting down' for fifty years, one door at a time. He was a bell-founder's apprentice. He warns: 'It rings to remember. It erases what won't answer.' Emotional beat: pity and terror.

chapters.title: 1974, In Someone Else's Coat
chapters.summary: Émile's POV. A flashback: young Émile and Wren's grandfather Marcel carry the clapper to the flooded well on a winter night, paid by men who wanted the village's guilt drowned with the bell. Emotional beat: complicity, the weight of a secret chosen over truth.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren locates the sealed well shaft and measures the waterline—rising fast with the spring melt. Days, not weeks. Meanwhile, a street Wren has mapped for years is simply gone from their own notebooks, erased in their handwriting. Emotional beat: panic, the horror of self-doubt.

chapters.title: Odile Remembers Everything
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, lucid for one hour. She tells Wren the truth: in 1911 the village melted the bell to hide a scandal—the drowning of a choir of children in the well during a flood the village ignored. The clapper was taken in 1974 when the ringing began again. Emotional beat: grief and inheritance of a terrible duty.

chapters.title: The Choir in the Water
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, tunnels. The bell rings again and the tunnels fill with children's voices singing a hymn no church uses anymore. Wren follows the song to the well and sees small hands beneath the surface, waiting. Emotional beat: heartbreak; the horror is sorrowful, not cruel.

chapters.title: Father Anselme's Bargain
chapters.summary: Father Anselme's POV. He confesses he has known for decades and has kept the village 'asleep' to protect it, feeding the bell small forgettings—names, dates—to keep it from ringing fully. He begs Wren to leave the clapper where it is. Emotional beat: love against duty, the antagonist's genuine tenderness.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren realizes the bell doesn't want the clapper back—it wants what the clapper was taken to silence: acknowledgment. But Émile insists the object itself must return to the water before the well refills, or the village drowns in memory all at once. Emotional beat: moral fork in the road.

chapters.title: The Village That Sleeps
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren walks the village at dusk and sees the erasure spreading: houses with no doors, neighbors who can't recall their children's names. Only Odile and Wren remain fully 'counted.' Emotional beat: loneliness, the cost of being the one who remembers.

chapters.title: Émile's Last Door
chapters.summary: Émile's POV. Émile reaches door number one of his fifty-year countdown and steps through it, finally at rest, leaving Wren his founder's ledger—the clapper's exact hiding place and a warning: 'It will offer you your grandfather instead.' Emotional beat: release and foreboding.

chapters.title: Marcel at the Waterline
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. In the tunnel by the well, the bell conjures Marcel, young and warm, who tells Wren he took the clapper to protect Wren's family, that truth would have destroyed them. Wren must decide whether love is a reason to keep a lie. Emotional beat: the novel's thematic crux, love against duty.

chapters.title: The Water Rises
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The meltwater floods the lower tunnels; Wren's maps dissolve to blank paper in the wet. Trapped between rising water and the thirteenth door, Wren chooses to go down toward the well rather than flee. Emotional beat: commitment—no way back but through.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, climax part one. Wren dives into the half-flooded well shaft and finds the clapper wedged beneath a child's rusted shoe. The drowned choir surrounds them, not menacing but waiting, singing Wren's own name—the one thing Wren could never keep written down. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into recognition.

chapters.title: Anselme at the Rope
chapters.summary: Father Anselme's POV. Above ground, Anselme holds the rope, torn between hauling Wren up and cutting it to preserve his fifty years of merciful forgetting. Odile, lucid, takes the rope from him. Emotional beat: an old man's surrender to a truth he feared.

chapters.title: The Ringing
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, climax. Wren hangs the clapper from the belfry beam by hand and strikes it once. The bell rings fully for the first time in a century; every erased name, date, and door floods back into the village at once, and the choir's voices rise with it and go quiet, remembered at last. Emotional beat: catharsis through unbearable fullness.

chapters.title: The Morning After Everything
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The village wakes remembering the drowned children, the scandal, and Marcel's crime. Some neighbors thank Wren; some cannot look at them. Odile's memory is clear and stays clear. Emotional beat: raw aftermath, truth's cost paid openly.

chapters.title: A New Register
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren and Father Anselme carve the children's names into a new parish register and cast a small memorial bell from Émile's ledger notes. Wren begins a new survey—one that maps what the village chose to forget as carefully as its tunnels. Emotional beat: mourning turned into stewardship.

chapters.title: Counting Forward
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, epilogue. A year later, Wren keeps counting doors—but now writes them down to remember, not to hide. On the anniversary, the new bell rings once, and Wren, standing in the belfry, answers it aloud. Emotional beat: peace earned, memory chosen over safety, love and truth reconciled.
